notes.b: Cooking and food preparation change protein in two linked steps. First the folded protein chain unfolds (denaturation), then the unfolded chains join up and set (coagulation). Both are permanent, and together they explain most of what happens to eggs, meat, fish and milk.
points: Denaturation is the irreversible unfolding of the secondary and tertiary structure of a protein (the folded shape of its chain), without breaking its peptide bonds (the links between amino acids), so the chain keeps its amino acids but changes shape.
Denatured chains lose the original shape and functional properties of the protein, because the function of a protein depends on its shape.
Denatured chains can then link to one another, and this linking is coagulation.
Coagulation is the setting of denatured protein into a solid or semi-solid mass, which is why a runny raw egg becomes firm when cooked.
Denaturation changes the texture and appearance of a food, and denatured protein is more digestible, so cooked protein foods are easier to digest than raw ones.
Denaturation can be caused by heat, mechanical action (such as whisking), chemicals (such as acid and salt) and enzymes.
Egg white coagulates from about 60 degrees C, turning from transparent to opaque and firm; the yolk sets at about 68 degrees C. These are approximate temperatures because eggs set over a range.
Fish flesh changes from translucent to opaque as its protein coagulates during cooking, which is how you can tell fish is cooked.
Examples of coagulation in cookery: omelette, quiche, boiled egg, meringue, soufflé and lemon meringue pie.
notes.tip: Say that denaturation is irreversible unfolding, without breaking peptide bonds, and that coagulation is the setting that follows. Name a dish with each property, such as egg white turning opaque at about 60 degrees C, a quiche or a meringue.

notes.b: A foam is a mass of air bubbles held in a thin film. Egg white makes a good foam because its protein, albumen, can be stretched into a film around each bubble and then set by heat.
points: Whisking or beating stretches and partly denatures the albumen chains, which unfold and arrange themselves around the air bubbles. This is mechanical action, not heat, that creates the foam.
The protein film around each bubble holds the trapped air, forming a foam.
Gentle heat in cooking then coagulates the albumen around the bubbles, setting the foam permanently, which is why a baked meringue stays firm.
Over-whisking denatures the protein too far and breaks the film, so the foam becomes grainy and collapses.
Examples: meringue, pavlova, soufflé and whisked sponge cake.
notes.tip: Foam formation is the whisking; coagulation by heat only fixes it, so do not say heat creates the foam. Give a culinary example such as meringue, pavlova, soufflé or sponge.

notes.b: A gel is a liquid held in a soft solid. Some proteins, especially gelatine, can do this: they dissolve in hot liquid and set into a network as it cools.
points: A gel forms when protein chains (gelatine) dissolved in a hot liquid cool and link into a network that traps the liquid, such as water.
Gelatine is the main protein used to make gels in cookery.
A firmer gel results from a higher concentration of gelatine, because more chains form a denser network.
Examples: jelly, aspic, mousses and cheesecake.
notes.tip: Gel formation here is protein (gelatine) setting a liquid, which is different from the gelatinisation of starch.

notes.b: Dry heat cooks food without added liquid. It acts mainly on the surface protein, which is why roasted and grilled foods firm up and brown.
points: Dry heat (roasting, baking, grilling and frying) denatures and coagulates the surface protein, causing shrinkage and firmness.
Prolonged dry heat dries the muscle protein and makes meat tough and dry, so overcooked meat is chewy.
Dry heat at high temperatures produces the Maillard reaction, which browns the surface of meat, bread and biscuits.
notes.tip: Excessive dry heat toughens meat, while moist heat tenderises it through collagen turning to gelatine; students often mix these up. For three effects of heat on protein foods, choose from coagulation, colour change, denaturation, more digestible, collagen to gelatine, softer meat, improved flavour and destroying micro-organisms.

notes.b: The golden-brown crust on bread and roast meat is not caused by sugar alone or by enzymes. It comes from protein and sugar reacting together under dry heat.
points: The Maillard reaction is non-enzymic browning, which happens when the amino acids of protein react with a reducing sugar (a sugar such as glucose) on heating.
It needs high heat and a dry surface with little moisture; it does not need enzymes.
It produces brown colour and roasted, savoury flavour, as in a toasted bread crust, roast meat, grilled or toasted cheese and biscuits.
notes.tip: Describe the Maillard reaction as non-enzymic browning, and remember it needs both protein and sugar. It is not caramelisation, which is sugar alone.

notes.b: Moist heat cooks food in liquid or steam at lower temperatures. For meat it does something dry heat cannot: it changes the tough connective tissue into a soft jelly.
points: Moist heat (boiling, stewing, poaching and braising) converts the collagen (the tough protein in connective tissue) to gelatine, which tenderises meat.
Collagen conversion needs long, slow cooking in moisture, so cheaper cuts of meat, which contain a lot of connective tissue, become tender.
Prolonged high heat toughens muscle protein, so gentle moist heat is used for tender results.
Heat breaks the weak bonds that hold the folded structure, which is why heat denatures protein.
notes.tip: Moist heat tenderises through collagen changing to gelatine. Say long, slow cooking for cheaper cuts.

notes.b: Whisking, beating and mincing physically stretch and break protein, so they change texture without any heat.
points: Whisking, beating and mincing unfold protein chains; whisking egg white is the example that forms a foam.
Kneading bread dough develops the gluten (the protein of wheat flour) into an elastic network that traps the carbon dioxide from yeast, so the dough rises.
Beating meat with a mallet breaks up the muscle fibres and tenderises it.
Excessive agitation denatures protein so far that it becomes tough or curdled.
notes.tip: Use whisking egg whites for meringue, sponge or soufflé as your example of mechanical action causing denaturation.

notes.b: Acids and salt change protein without any heating. That is why a splash of lemon juice curdles milk and a marinade softens meat.
points: Acids such as lemon juice and vinegar denature protein; lemon juice added to milk curdles it, which is also how milk sours.
A marinade of acid, such as vinegar, wine or lemon, tenderises meat by denaturing its surface protein.
Alkalis also denature protein and change its texture.
Cheese-making uses acid to help set the milk protein, and salt to increase the firmness of the curd (the solid part of the milk), which controls the texture of the cheese.
The acid in the stomach denatures food protein before enzymes hydrolyse (break) it, so the chains are easier for digestive enzymes to reach.
notes.tip: For a cause of denaturation with an example, acid gives cheese-making, vinegar tenderising meat or souring milk, and salt gives cheese-making.

notes.b: Enzymes are biological catalysts, and some of them work on protein. Cooks use them to set milk for cheese and to soften tough meat.
points: Rennin, traditionally from the stomach of young calves, coagulates casein (the main protein of milk) for cheese-making.
Papain, from papaya, is a proteolytic enzyme (one that breaks down protein) that tenderises tough meat.
Proteolytic enzymes hydrolyse peptide bonds, so too much enzyme action makes protein soft and mushy.
Enzymes in the digestive tract hydrolyse protein to amino acids.
Heat inactivates enzymes, which is why cooking stops enzymic tenderising.
notes.tip: Name the enzyme with its job: rennin coagulates casein in cheese-making, and papain tenderises meat.

notes.h: Investigation: heat and whisking on egg white
notes.b: This investigation shows denaturation in practice by comparing egg white that is left alone, heated and whisked.
points: Aim: to show how heat and mechanical action denature egg white protein.
Independent variable: the treatment (heating in a water bath, or whisking); dependent variable: the change in appearance and texture of the white.
Controlled variables: the same volume of egg white, the same starting temperature and the same type of dish.
Control: place an untreated sample of egg white in a labelled dish for comparison.
Method: heat a second sample gently in a water bath until it sets, then whisk a third sample until stiff.
Safety: use fresh eggs, wash hands after handling raw egg, and do not taste raw egg white, because raw egg can carry bacteria.
Expected result: the heated white turns opaque and firm, and the whisked white forms a stable foam; the untreated white stays clear and runny.
Conclusion: heat and whisking both denature the protein of egg white and change its appearance and texture.

keyTerms.definition: The irreversible unfolding of a protein's secondary and tertiary structure, without breaking its peptide bonds.
The setting of denatured protein chains, which link together to form a solid or semi-solid mass.
The trapping of air bubbles in a protein film when egg white is whisked, with gentle heat fixing the foam.
The formation of a network of protein chains that traps water when a hot protein solution cools.
Non-enzymic browning of protein and reducing sugar on heating, giving brown colour and roasted flavour.
Softening meat by breaking down its muscle fibres or connective tissue, using mechanical action, moist heat, acid or enzymes.
An enzyme from the stomach of young calves that coagulates casein in milk.
An enzyme that hydrolyses the peptide bonds of protein, such as papain.
A derived protein formed when collagen is heated in moisture; it sets to a gel on cooling.

questions.prompt: Outline how mechanical action and acid each cause protein to change during food preparation, giving one example of each.
questions.model: Mechanical action: whisking or beating unfolds the protein chains, which arrange around air bubbles to form a foam; example: whisked egg white for a meringue. Acid: denatures the protein and can cause coagulation; example: lemon juice curdles milk, or vinegar in a marinade tenderises meat.

questions.prompt: Explain the effect of dry heat, moist heat, mechanical action and enzymes on protein during the preparation and cooking of food. Describe the Maillard reaction in your answer.
questions.model: Dry heat: denatures surface protein, causing shrinkage and firmness; prolonged dry heat makes meat tough; high temperatures produce the Maillard reaction. Maillard reaction: non-enzymic browning of protein and reducing sugar on heating, giving brown colour and roasted flavour; it needs high heat and a dry surface. Moist heat: converts collagen to gelatine, tenderising meat when cooked slowly; prolonged high heat toughens muscle protein. Mechanical action: whisking forms a foam; kneading develops an elastic gluten network; beating tenderises meat. Enzymes: rennin coagulates casein in cheese-making; papain tenderises meat; proteolytic enzymes hydrolyse protein, making it soft if overused; heat inactivates enzymes.
